He said: Madam Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity to start the debate on the motion you just read, which is in my name, and perhaps may read it
again:
That this House condemn the govemments's mismanagement, lack of leadership, incompetence and negligence that has placed Canada's fishing communitites and workers in unparalleled jeopardy.
Madam Speaker, I also want to take this opportunity to point to the many shortcomings in this Government's policies where the interests of the fishing communities on the West Coast, the Great Lakes and the East Coast are concerned. I would like to start by discussing the problems on the West Coast, especially those problems that will arise as a of the decision by the binational panel on Pacific salmon and herring, landings. Many jobs are at stake. Jobs are in jeopardy and jobs will be lost. On November 17, the Minister said in Richmond, and perhaps I may recall his words:

"I give my assurances that these jobs are safe". [Translation]
He wanted to reassure these people by saying that no jobs would be lost as result of the FTA.

As my colleague the member for Winnipeg South Centre remarked on June 15, the Conservative government could have protected the west coast fishery by not putting it and all these jobs on the free trade bargaining table.
Today I wish to demonstrate to this House, to the thousands of people who are listening in the fishery
October 19, 1989

industry, and to Canadians in general how this government put our west coast jobs at risk, as well as jobs on the east coast.
Article 1801 states:
Disputes arising under both this agreement and General Agreement on Tariffs and Hade and agreements negotiated thereunder may be settled in either forum, according to the rules of that forum, at the discretion of the complaining party.
In other words, the U.S. has the choice to challenge any trade practice in either the GATT or the free trade agreement. Naturally it will choose whichever forum is to its advantage.
If the U.S. chooses to challenge under GATT rules, the free trade agreement clearly states in article 408 that Canada cannot use export taxes to protect domestic industries such as the west coast fisheries. It reads as follows:
Neither party shall maintain or introduce any tax, duty, or charge on the export of any good to the territory of the other party, unless such tax, duty, or charge is also maintained or introduced on such good when destined for domestic consumption.
Export taxes to protect domestic industries have been a recognized practice under the GATT. As my colleague from Winnipeg South Centre said on June 15, it is perfectly legitimate to use an export tax so that non-pro-cessed fish from Canada is subject to a higher tax. However, the government has decided that we could do without this unique and potent remedy. This is sheer stupidity.
The next time we hear this government saying that it is through no fault of its own that the GATT rules apply, we will know that it is not telling the whole truth. They have castrated the GATT rules by removing the most effective remedy, the only one that could have helped Canada protect those jobs in the west coast fishing industry.
To summarize, this government has signed a deal which gives the United States of America the right to choose its weapon, the free trade agreement or the GATT. If the U.S. chooses the GATT, this government has chosen to abandon the only GATT consistent remedy of any significance, the right to impose an export tax. This has led to the free trade panel ruling by which Canada has lost its power to impose processing and landing requirements. This means that Canadians will

lose jobs and that Canada can no longer establish job creating policies for Canadians.
We have not even started to speak about conserving our resource. With this ruling we can no longer take measures of conservation. This ruling says that we cannot apply landing requirements to 10 per cent or 20 per cent, that part of the fisheries which will be exported. How are we to determine just what is 10 per cent or 20 per cent? We will find out after the fact when it will be too late.
As I stated earlier, in 1987 the minister of fisheries said that he would save those jobs. Two days ago he said that he did know how many jobs would be lost. On the one hand he says that it is a victory for Canada, and on the other hand he says that he is going to take 30 days to consider. Then his colleague in the Senate, the government leader in the Upper House, Senator Lowell Murray, contradicts the minister and says that the government accepts the finding and intends to work within the context of that finding.
Confusion is the major problem in the fisheries. There is confusion from this government. We do not know who leads the fisheries. When we talk about overfishing, it is External Affairs; when we talk about free trade, it is the Minister for International Trade; and then, the leader in the Senate intervenes once in awhile. Who is in charge?
Nobody.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is not the only instance where the Conservative Government failed to take a firm stand on defending our interests in the fisheries industry. The case of drift net fishing on the West Coast is another example. The Americans have the same problem but have taken a much firmer stand and obtained far better results.
If we look at the Great Lakes fisheries, it's the same story. The Great Lakes fisheries also have problems like water pollution and acid rain which affect the quality of the fish.
Madam Speaker, you will agree that the Government has been guilty of mismanagement as far as the West Coast and Great Lakes fisheries are concerned.

I would now like to look at the situation on the Atlantic coast. The problems facing the Atlantic Provinces do not concern just one minister. In fact, the entire Cabinet is responsible.
All this started a while ago. More than 1,200 jobs were cut at the CN workshops. The Tories are now going to make cuts in VIA Rail, and we will lose hundreds of jobs. The Tories have refused to take part in a joint program with the provinces for improving existing municipal infrastructures.
The Conservatives are going to make cuts in the Unemployment Insurance Program, after we were given the assurance there would no cuts. The Tories are going to make more cutbacks and close bases, especially the base at Summerside. Thousands of jobs will be lost.
Now they are asking us to approve a 9 per cent tax on goods and services. And as if that were not enough, on top of it all, they refuse to acknolwedge there is a crisis in the fisheries industry. This is simply too much! When fishermen, plant owners and workers and all the people who depend on the fisheries industry call for help, the Government, through the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, says that this year is a good year, that things aren't that bad and that the fishermen are pretty well off!
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans, with the approval of its Minister, has the gall to publish a document that describes the current situation as the best we ever had. This is utterly absurd!
Madam Speaker, the Minister is aware of the fact that a number of fish stocks are in danger of disappearing. First of all, our northern cod, and there is also the crab in the Gulf and the lobster situation.
The preliminary report prepared by Dr. Harris suggests various ways of dealing with a crisis that is imminent, a fact that the Minister refuses to acknowledge. Furthermore, the Minister keeps repeating there is surplus capacity on the East Coast and that the number of vessels has doubled since 1986. What he does not say is that the Tories allowed this surplus capacity to build up. They do not say that all the decisions since 1984 were made by the Tories. This Government must take the blame for the surplus capacity.

This government does not know what it is doing. Here is another example of confusion. On May 11, the Minister for International Trade hinted at help for fishermen, communities, and plant workers, and told reporters that the impact of further cuts would be comparable to last year's drought on western and Ontario farmers, who had been promised a $1 billion aid program.
The same day the Minister of Fisheries said: "We will be deciding on a comprehensive way of dealing with the problem". Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs commented that it is a very serious problem.
How is that, Madam Speaker, from a government that says fishermen are having a good year, as the Minister for Fisheries insisted on October 2 in this House? The same minister is now saying that there is no real emergency, there is no need for an aid package, and that existing programs are adequate. You will hear from my colleagues from Atlantic Canada who will tell this House how inadequate those programs are, Madam Speaker.
This government is showing a sense of irresponsibility, especially when it comes to the well-being of Canadians and especially Atlantic Canadians.
This government is trying to convince Canadians that the problems are not as serious as they are in reality. We know that in late December, when we are out of this House, reductions in cod quotas will be announced. These reductions will mean a loss of revenue for the fishermen. It will mean a loss of jobs for the plant workers. Communities that depend on those stocks will lose their economic base. What does this government, this minister, do? He turns a deaf ear. He is not prepared to come to the rescue.
Unemployment is also a very good example of the short-sightedness of this government. The Minister of Employment and Immigration wants to retrain the unemployed in Atlantic Canada. I have been saying that it makes no sense because there are no other jobs to retrain for, and that consequently the people we retrain will have to leave the area. This is a massive relocation program, that is what it is.
This program has been questioned, not only by the members of the opposition, but also by the Minister of Fisheries who, on May 12, in an interview with the Chronicle-Herald was quoted as saying: "It's tough in Atlantic Canada to talk about retraining or restructuring

entire communities. You can't treat it", speaking about the fishing industry, "like a bolt factory closing in Toronto". That is exactly what we have been saying, the types of training programs that are proposed will not do the job.
The numbers do not lie. There is a problem in the fishery. What is lacking is a government with the necessary courage to address the problem right away, not wait until later on. In this crisis we must remember the fishermen, the plant workers, the small fishing communities. They do not have the strength or the capacity of the bigger corporations. At least one-third of the labour force in Nova Scotia's small fishing communities, which amount to about 150,000 people, are employed in the fishing industry.
Overfishing is also a plague. How can we ask our own fishermen to make sacrifices when some countries, some members of the European community overfish to the tune of ten times their allocated quotas. Canadians are asking for an end to this overfishing. They are asking that we extend our jurisdiction so that we can control those stocks. All Atlantic Canadians are asking the government to take some kind of action, and still this government refuses to act.
Finally, I come back to the beginning. In addition to all the problems that this government does not want to deal with, we must add the possibility that the Americans will want to access our east coast just like they are doing on the west coast. It is only a matter of time. They will access it either through recent legislation, as in the case of lobsters, or through GATT, since this government has stripped GATT of any remedy. There is no stopping the U.S. It is only a question of time.

Madam Speaker, of course I would have liked to spend some more time on the problems in my riding and the entire province of New Brunswick, such as the decline in crab stocks, lobster prices and lobster catches, and also, if I may digress somewhat, on the economic policies of this Government which go against the interests of our fishermen, and I am referring to the Government's policy of high interest rates which keeps the Canadian dollar at a relatively high level compared to the US dollar and makes our exports less competitive. That is

exactly what is happening to our lobster. We can't sell it. Our fishermen had to catch it and sell it for practically nothing: $1.50 a pound. And the Minister and the Government still refuse to act.
Madam Speaker, my colleagues will describe these problems in detail when they speak later on, and I am sure the people of Beausejour will recognize the situations and will conclude, as I have concluded, that although we cannot do much about the vagaries of mother nature, in some areas it is possible to find solutions and to take action, something this Government has refused to do.
Madam Speaker, what fishermen and workers in the fisheries industry want is a minister who understands them, a minister who goes out and meets and talks to them and listens, so he will be better able to defend the interests of these communities. hon. member think that the requests of the government of Newfoundland should be acceded to?
What they are saying is this, and I quote from the executive report of the summary: "The problems we are facing in 1990 are a direct result of the resource crisis". Madam Speaker, I was interested in the remarks that the member for Beausejour made about the problem posed by unprocessed fish leaving Canada and being processed in other places, particularly in the United States of America. That happens on the Atlantic coast as well as the Pacific coast. The solution that the member mentioned was an export tax. As I understand his presentation, we should have kept the ability to put export taxes on unprocessed fish leaving Canada.
What I want to comment on so everybody will know, is that the people who are exporting that unprocessed fish out of Canada are Canadians. I want to know whether the member has spoken to those Canadian fishermen and fish brokers and told them that he thinks there should be an export tax on the products that they are exporting. I wonder if he has discussed it with them and has their consent to that kind of tax imposition.
I would also like to know what the member has to say about the possible repercussions of imposing such a tax. Is it not possible that the people in the countries that are adversely affected by such a tax might look at our situation and perhaps take retaliatory action? What is he going to do if that action is taken? What is he going to do if fish products from Canada are banned or taxed in some other way? Now, reflecting on these two points, I want to ask the member, does he still think export taxes solve problems?

Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Madam Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member for Beausejour initiated this important debate in the House of Commons today. It is not that I agree with the stark language of the motion, but I think this is a very important subject which is too often ignored in the House of Commons and across the nation. It is of extreme importance to the people of Atlantic and Pacific Coast Canada and the inland waters where commercial fisheries are also important.
I want to say to my colleague, the hon. member for Nepean, that she or her party have no monopoly on concern.
We take our responsibilities to the fishermen and the fishing communities of Canada extremely seriously.
At the present time there are a number of troubles in the Atlantic Canadian fishery, most not of the making of governments, but due to other circumstances over which we should exercise a different kind of control perhaps than we have in the past, but there are a number of troubles which must be addressed and this debate will give us a chance to discuss them.
These difficulties have to be discussed in a sensitive and caring fashion because they pose a great amount of anxiety and worry for the people who depend on the fishery and, indeed, if they are not addressed there could be genuine areas of hardship in the months ahead.
I want to take part of my time to point out that there is no crisis in the fishery. The crisis emanates from those who would exaggerate alarm and suggest that, contrary to the fact, throughout Canada there is some kind of great chaos when indeed the opposite is true, and the management of Canada's fisheries is sound.
There is no government before us in recent times that has devoted more effort to enriching and improving our vital fisheries resources. No government before us has ever considered the state of the fisheries as carefully, no government has ever included fisheries as high on the priority list of cabinet.
The record of this government in the area of fisheries is one of responsible, intelligent and sensitive management of an important and valued resource. The government knows, and everyone should know, there are no

October 19, 1989
Supply
shortcuts to managing a healthy, natural resource so that sustainable development becomes a reality, not just a goal to which lip service is paid when it is convenient.
This government has taken strong measures to keep the fisheries vital and in consequence we have had years of unprecedented growth, a thriving industry, and maximum profits up to the end of 1988. The fishery is changing and we have to recognize that the fishery has undergone cyclic change many times through its history, and that change is also part of reality. New fishing technologies, shifts in the environmental conditions globally, market forces, the unpredictability of nature, the supply of fish from other sources in other lands, all these factors have contributed to the state of flux and, therefore, the state of anxiety on the part of Canadian fisheries, particularly in Atlantic Canada.
We are honestly and intelligently addressing that change. This means we are taking an objective look at the state of our fisheries to ensure that vision and reality merge to provide a healthy resource for today and for generations to come.
To do this we must explore, develop and adopt policies which can maintain a viable and productive resource for the future. This government does not endorse benign neglect when it comes to renewable resources. This government, unlike hon. members opposite sometimes, does not endorse merely taking short-term measures when we expect a long-term steady gain and improvement in the fisheiy. It just does not work that way.
Scientific research, consultation among all players, and judicious management of fish stocks are the keys to a prosperous resource. This takes time and special expertise. Putting all this together is what constitutes an intelligent management of the resource.
The fact is that conservation and the need to avoid overfishing involves difficult choices. We have an overarching commitment to resource management and to sustaining economic utilization of a well-managed fishery. In this regard, Canada stands at the top of the list among nations when it comes to the refinement of methodology for stock assessment, the establishment of quotas, and devising an effective protective process for living within those quotas that amounts to sound management decisions.
I am pleased to say that all in all, the professionalism of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the
sometimes cautious but realistic way in which we have managed stocks has led to many significant gains for the industry.
Let us examine some of the facts. For Atlantic Canada alone, from 1983 to 1988, landings of all fish species increased by 200,000 tonnes to 1.3 million tonnes over that period of only five years. Total added value increased by $400 million to over $1 billion during the same period. The total value of processed fish products increased by three-quarters of a billion to $2.2 billion in 1988. Our management program has resulted in more than two and one-half times as much cod in the sea now than there was when we took over management of the fisheries.
In Scotia-Fundy, lobster landings have more tripled, from 5,133 tonnes in 1978 to 15,335 tonnes in 1987. The landed value of lobster increased more than five times, from $28 million in 1983 to $143 million in 1988. In the scallop industry, which is again showing strong returns this year, it looks like this year's catch will exceed last year's record levels and there are still three months of fishing left.
This year's bluefin tuna fishery in Atlantic Canada has turned into a bumper year. Our inshore fishermen have landed nearly $10 million worth of tuna since the middle of August. We, for the first time in memory, will use the full Canadian quota. Canada is developing a name for itself as a supplier of high-quality tuna to the international marketplace.
The success has not been limited to one coast alone. In the Pacific we have had the largest sockeye salmon run this year, in 85 years. We have rebuilt the stocks in the herring fishery from 13,000 tonnes in 1986 to 35,000 tonnes today. For the continued growth of all our fisheries, we have instituted a national habitat policy, a model for the world to emulate, which provides certainty in the growth of the industry and a balance among competing interests for development. We have had ongoing success with our program of enterprise allocations and we are introducing individual vessel quotas on an experimental basis at the present time in Atlantic Canada.
Now I ask you, does all this not suggest something other than gross mismanagement as the opposition charges?

I want to take a few minutes here then to describe, in more detail, the current situation in the Atlantic fishery, a situation which is very complex and is not amenable to a quick fix, short-term approach which the hon. members opposite are wont to put forward.
The fact is that, based on our professional scientific assessments, we have been able to develop and enlarge the potential of the Atlantic fishery enormously. In recent years we have experienced very strong gains, but new factors and pressures, the wild cards, if you will, have had different effects on the Atlantic fishery.
These include the impact of technology on the resource; that is, the improved boats and techniques of fishermen and the capacity that is accumulated with that, and the real effect of a changing environment in the northwest Atlantic on the quality and the accuracy of our predicative techniques.
Combine this with the fact that healthy profits of the last two years have been eroded by global market changes, by shifts in exchange rates and by significant declines in prices, and you begin to understand the new context in which the fishery must be managed for the future.
This is the context, this ever-changing environment, the entire environment, markets, the resource base, the capacity, the technology, and the effect it has on people. It is this context, that of change, that we must manage.
We have taken already a number of important concrete steps. In the almost four years that I have been Minister of Fisheries, I have met close to three dozen times with my Atlantic fisheries colleagues. I meet regularly with industry and a host of advisory groups. We have availed ourselves of all the expertise and resources at our disposal to explore every dimension of this issue. We have brought initiatives forward which were endorsed at the First Ministers' Conference in November, 1986.1 visited Atlantic Canada in the summer of 1986, as I do each summer. I walked the wharfs, went to see the fishermen, and witnessed a deterioration in the northern cod inshore fishery. So I took specific measures, starting in the summer of 1986, to change the fishing practices of the offshore fleet, to reduce quotas, to reduce the wastage by discards at sea, and to require observers on all domestic vessels fishing in that offshore fishery.
Supply
We went further. We appointed the independent Alverson Commission of eminent international scientists to review our own scientific methodology so that we might be sure we had it right. That, coupled with new enforcement initiatives, helicopter patrols and much increased fines under the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, have all contributed to an updated and more effective means of assessing the northern cod stocks which are such an important and fundamental part of the Atlantic fishery. This gives some of the background to the problem that faces us today.
However, in light of declining quotas and changing world market conditions we have had to take additional measures. I want to describe four special initiatives we have taken. The first is the establishment of a special committee of senior ministers, chaired by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to develop and co-ordinate the government's response on the state of the northern cod fishery and other Atlantic fisheries issues. Through this committee, cabinet is reviewing the adequacy of existing programs to help communities that might be affected by all the factors I have just described, and is poised to act quickly upon the solutions best suited to the task. I am pleased that my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration and other members of that committee are coming up with some very interesting and innovative ideas as to how to deal with this. I will leave it to my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, to describe later today how we will address some of these social conditions and how we will look, over the next few months, to special assistance for the fishermen of the Newfoundland region, as we have done for areas within the fishery where important social assistance was required.
I recognize, as does this government, that from time to time there are problems in the fishery. Lord knows, that is the nature of my existence. There is not a new morning that dawns but what there are one or more new problems to be addressed. Some of these are large problems, some are smaller, and more localized. This government is addressing all these problems, working with the industry and all of those affected to provide appropriate solutions for fishermen and their families in fishing communities throughout Atlantic Canada. I assure them that the Prime Minister and all of the ministers of this government are deeply concerned. That is why the government is devoting significant resources to deal with the problem.

October 19, 1989
Supply
The Harris Panel, a second initiative on northern cod, is again examining all the scientific techniques used in the stock assessment process. By the end of the year, I look forward to receiving the final report of the Harris Panel, which will give us input to the quota-setting process for 1990.
Third, a Scotia-Fundy task force, which I recently established, is exploring all aspects of fishing and fish processing in the Scotia-Fundy area, where we have far too little added value. We are exporting too much raw fish, with the consent and encouragement, very often, of local government. We have to change that; we have to deal with the over-capacity in the Scotia-Fundy fishery. That is why I have asked for this special Scotia-Fundy task force to meet with fishermen, travel to communities, and report back to the special cabinet committee.
Finally, we have made foreign overfishing a government priority of the highest order, as reflected in the Throne Speech of last spring. Foreign overfishing in the Atlantic, on the nose and tail of the Grand Banks, and also foreign overfishing on the Pacific by the indiscriminate use of high seas drift nets threaten to endanger international high sea fish stocks on a global scale. It is this overfishing, which is wreaking havoc on the life cycle of the northwest Atlantic fishery. It is depleting the straddling stocks that live both within and beyond our jurisdiction.
The European community has abstained from supporting the quotas set out by the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, a voluntary international body that regulates fishing quotas, and will go ahead and set their own quotas outside Canada's 200-mile limit, if all Canadians do not stand up and express their outrage, as we have been doing in various forums, for the past six months.
I have travelled abroad, as have other ministers, in the United States and Europe, giving this message that we must halt this intolerable practice of overfishing Canadian groundfish stocks.
In the meetings of the OECD in July, the Prime Minister raised these overfishing problems directly and forcefully. A new campaign launched last week by my colleague, the Minister of International Trade, takes our
case directly and forcefully to the European people, appealing to their sensitivity and concern for global environmental practices, which threaten the very future of the living resources on which we depend.
All these honest efforts to deal with the changing realities of the Atlantic fishery are proof of our concern and commitment to the well-being of our fishing communities and our resource, the backbone of the economy.
That is not all. We have added $3 million to our scientific program of stock assessment on northern cod, an increase of 80 per cent over last year. We will be providing additional funds for aerial surveillance and enforcement. I hope to have details forthcoming in a few weeks on the new surveillance program that we will be initiating on both coasts. As well, over the next few months, I will announce an aquaculture strategy which will bring a new dimension and untold benefit to the coastal regions of Canada.
We can talk about incompetence and mismanagement, but overfishing is not practised by the Government of Canada or ministers. It is practised by fishermen, whether foreign or Canadian. We must end this wastage of the resource and the inaccuracy it introduces to our scientific stock assessment process.
We must bring it under control by introducing amendments to the Fisheries Act which will significantly increase fines for infractions committed under our Canadian fisheries legislation. Fines, which are presently limited to $5,000, must be raised to more realistic levels commensurate with the magnitude of the benefit to be gained from crimes against the fishery.
I seek the co-operation of members on all sides of the House to support the speedy passage of this package of initiatives, which I hope to bring to the House soon.
I would like to take time to deal with the Pacific fishery and the recent free trade panel decision which Canada has not yet accepted. I see that my time is running to an end but I want to assure Canadians and members of this House that, first of all, we are examining this FTA panel report very carefully. We have never claimed it to be a victory. I do not know why the press and the opposition persist in using the word "victory" or "win" to describe it, although there is much editorial opinion to that effect.
October 19, 1989

The headline in The Vancouver Province yesterday stated that it is a net gain for Canada. The Ottawa Citizen yesterday stated, "Fish trade ruling pragmatic." Yesterday's Montreal Gazette said of the free trade panel ruling:
Chalk up one success for the Canada-U.S. free trade deal-the panel decision, which is non-binding, seems to be a good one in principle. And there seems to be no reason to think Canada would have got a better deal from a GATT panel if the dispute had been resolved there.
I am not coming to that conclusion. We have taken note of the facts and the decision of the free trade panel on which three of the five members were Canadians. The sovereignty of Canada takes precedence over all other factors in terms of ensuring that we have the scientific data, the necessary information, biological information, weight and size information which we must use as a basis for managing the fishery.
Therefore, in establishing whether or not some quantity of fish might be allowed to be exported by sea, the Minister of Fisheries, under Canadian fisheries legislation, will , have the final say to ensure that all means of transport, all means of taking fish from our fishing grounds are subject to full management control in accordance with our scientific objectives. That was the purpose of the new landing requirements that we brought into effect last May, I believe, it was. Those regulations were brought in to replace discriminatory protectionist measures restricting the export of unprocessed salmon and herring which were found unacceptable by the international General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs council because they gave Canada protection that our American neighbours did not enjoy. We have dismantled those regulations, because as a fish exporting nation, our markets must remain open. Eighty per cent of our fisheries production goes into international markets. For members to suggest trade restriction or protectionist practices as the way to protect jobs in Canada is to ignore the fact that those jobs are never secure unless the markets to which the fish is destined remain open.

Madam Speaker, I have one question for the Minister of Fisheries. It relates to what he was talking about, quotas and Canadian jurisdiction.
National Sea Products recently came to this government, because this government is a shareholder in that company, and said that they were soon going to announce the closure of two more fish plants, one in Newfoundland and one in Cape Breton, because of reduced quotas. Those fish plants would likely be either

Canso or Louisburg. They also said that if it were Canso, it would mean the loss of 700 jobs inside the plant, plus eight trawlers tied up. In the case of St. John's, Newfoundland, the other plant mentioned, 450 inshore workers would lose their jobs and several trawlers tied up in Newfoundland.
How can the minister allow a reduction in quotas to these Canadian companies, with announcements coming of more lay-offs in the fisheries in Newfoundland and in Nova Scotia, when he has allotted to the Japanese 3,000 metric tonnes of red fish inside our 200-mile zone right now; 5,000 metric tonnes of halibut inside our our 200-mile zone right now; and, for the Russians, cod inside our 200-mile zone right now-red fish and halibut to 12,000 metric tonnes. That is 20,000 metric tonnes of fish, the very fish that is processed in those two plants in St. John's, and in Canso. Why does the minister not kick the foreigners out of our waters instead of kicking Canadians out of their jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the drama in his question. That is the member's style. But he has a clever way of manipulating numbers to his own advantage.
I think the hon. member knows, but probably would not want to tell the House himself, that we do not make any stocks available to foreign fishing vessels within our 200-mile economic limit, unless they are surplus to the requirements of the Canadian industry, whether it be inshore or offshore. Now hold your seat, my friend. We do not make non-surplus stocks available. Canadian fishing companies always have first option to access those stocks.
The only fishery by foreign vessels within Canadian waters is for surplus fish that the Canadian companies, the Canadian fishermen, the Canadian markets, and our export markets are not interested in. I want to point out to the hon. member who sat as a member of a government for several years that ignored the problem of foreign fishing in our zone, that, in fact, his government allowed the European Community to harvest 10,000 tonnes of prime cod stocks and other prime groundfish stocks in our waters and allowed the French fleet to fish within the Gulf of St. Lawrence to a level of 17,000 tonnes over and above the needs of St. Pierre and Miquelon. We have ended those practices. We have eliminated the 17,000 tonnes of fishing by the French metropolitan fleet and we have removed all fishing by European nations from within our waters on the non-

Supply
surplus stocks, which are necessary for our own fishing fleets.
The Hon. Member knows that. I wish he would stop alarming the people of his area by suggesting that somehow foreign overfishing is the heart of the problem within the 200-mile zone. We have fixed that. We brought in helicopter surveillance. We brought in fines up to $750,000 for offences by foreign vessels within our waters. The Liberal government did not have the courage to do that. We ended the long-term agreement with the European community. We ended the agreement that the Liberals had perpetuated from 1972 allowing the French trawlers within our waters. We have found a means of solving once and for all the boundary problem around St. Pierre and Miquelon which will bring untold benefit, when it is finally resolved, to the fishermen of Newfoundland. The hon. member has the gall to get up and condemn this government when it was the Liberal government that caused these problems.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister spent a fair amount of time talking about the management of the resource which is at the heart of a healthy industry, if we have the capacity to manage the resource in perpetuity. I wonder if he would tell the House how the recent judgment made by the FTA panel enables Canada to protect the jobs of Canadians and manage the resource in such a way that in perpetuity we will have a resource that we can count on for Canadian jobs. He might also want to comment on the virtue of an export tax on the product.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is some confusion about the purpose for which the new landing requirements were introduced earlier this year. For many years there was an export restriction on unprocessed sockeye and pink salmon and herring from the west coast of Canada, but no such restriction on the other species of salmon, Chinook, the coho and the chum species. These are very important, not only to our commercial fishery on the west coast, but they are a prized fish within the five species of salmon. This is also a very important sport fishery, and a recreational interest to Canadians.
In March 1987, Canada accepted the findings of the GATT panel that the old export restrictions gave Canada certain protection which was not in the nature of a fair-trade practice. We removed those and brought in last May, new requirements that all salmon and herring caught on the Pacific coast be landed at registered landing stations to be counted, graded, weighed, and sampled from a biological perspective so that we would have more effective control. We need good records and accurate information on which to base the scientific estimates and the establishment of quotas.
This set of landing regulations has been upheld with a slight modification in recognition of the paramountcy of Canada in deciding the way in which we should regulate the export of our fish. This relates to the possibility of some fishermen taking their fish directly to U.S. processing ports, rather than bringing it to shore in Canada first. The panel report found that a small proportion of the fish might be allowed to be shipped directly, as is often done in Atlantic Canada. That has been done with other species on the Pacific coast. We oppose the notion that we should not have control of 100 per cent of the species landed. The FTA panel agreed with Canada's position that a state could not be obliged to make its fisheries conservation and management regime dependent on co-operation with another state.
That overrides and gives to the Minister of Fisheries the authority to be the final say as to whether any fish should be allowed to be shipped by sea. I can assure this House of our interest in conservation and long-term stable management of the salmon resource, which we built up to record levels of production from a very low point in 1913 when we had a great slide on the Fraser Canyon. We will use the powers of the Fisheries Act, the Fish Inspection Act, and the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act to ensure that the resource is well managed by having full access to the necessary scientific information no matter what means of transport when fish is sold from Canada.
I should point out that many experts and some representatives of the Pacific coast fishing industry welcome this decision because it gives them a choice as fishermen to get the highest price for their fish. They are not forced to sell to a cartel of a certain small number of processing plants in Canada. A very prominent former Royal commissioner and candidate for the Liberal Party said only yesterday, and I would like to quote Dr. Peter
October 19, 1989

Pearse: "Fishermen should be allowed to sell their catch wherever they can get the highest price. If fishermen can get more value out of them and pay a higher price than domestic processors we won't get the maximum value out of the fish by processing them at home."
In answer to my hon. colleague from Surrey-White Rock, I just want to say that we are confident that the panel report-I am not in any way fettering the powers of Canada and the Minister of Fisheries-is going to prove, if we accept it, to be an improvement, notwithstanding the fact that we would prefer to have 100 per cent landing of our fish at Canadian ports.

Madam Speaker, I shall start with a question which the minister in his good time may answer. I think the minister would agree that what the panel really decided was that our regulations, as they now stand, are contrary to the free trade act regulations.
If we want to submit a new regulation it would then have to go through the process again. If we said we need 95 per cent or 90 per cent or even 60 per cent to manage the resource, that would have to be again adjudicated to see whether or not they agreed this was a proper percentage. In all likelihood there would be different people on the panel. I do not think we are in a very safe position having the minister read from the body of the report. It is the recommendation or conclusion of the report that counts, not the discussion in the body of the report. I have read the report, and the conclusion as well.
I take no pleasure at all in supporting the Liberal Party's motion at this time-more in sorrow than in tiying to get political advantage from criticizing. I have been personally aware, having lived on the west coast in Nanaimo all my life, of mismanagement, lack of leadership, incompetence, and negligence with respect to the fishing industry for the last 50 years of my life. Not only has it placed the Canadian fishing communities in unparalleled jeopardy, but it threatens the long-term protection of an invaluable sustainable resource.
It is not something that has been done deliberately or through lack of knowledge, but rather often through use of the wrong knowledge. I can recall some 40 years ago when I discussed with a fisherman on the west coast advice coming from the Department of Fisheries and
Supply
Oceans to the effect that herring was totally unlimited. It was impossible to overfish that resource. And the fishermen knew better. They were warning these officials that they were taking too much herring out of the water. Of course the officials, the experts, knew better. I think it was just three years after that before they had to impose controls because they were seriously depleting the herring resource.
The minister quoted examples this morning of individual successes and said, "Doesn't this prove that there has been proper management in the last five years". The minister knows better than that. If there is proper management, it had to go back more than five years in order to rebuild some of the runs that were so seriously damaged, at least on the west coast. It goes back a lot further than that.
Nevertheless, using as examples a few successes and omitting to mention all of the failures makes me wonder whether it is good luck or good management. The minister, for example, did not mention the serious depletion of the halibut resources on the west coast, and I have heard halibut resources on the east coast talked about here. He has not mentioned serious depletions of other species on the west coast where I understand his own ministry is likely to impose total closure for at least one year, and I am not sure how many more years. That is not known yet, as I understand. We will wait until that happens.
There is serious depletion of some species on the west coast and there certainly is on the east coast. I was at Lockeport. I took the time to go there and listen to some of those people who have lost their jobs. Twenty odd million dollars of provincial and federal money was put in that processing plant which was closed down through lack of product at the same time as we are shipping roundfish to the States and, as the other members have told us about, to Europe as well. Fishermen are coming over and taking it.
The minister has said that we must get together and continue to express our outrage internationally at what is happening to our fish stocks. Those expressions of outrage, along with 80 cents, will get you a cup of coffee in the parliamentary cafeteria. That is about all it has achieved to date. We have not achieved any co-operation

internationally in looking after our very valuable resource.
To come perhaps a little more up to date with respect to what has happened recently, the minister said that Canada accepted the GATT ruling in March of 1987. I believe he would like to make that March of 1988. I do not think I have his attention right now, but it was actually in March of 1988 rather than 1987 that Canada accepted the GATT ruling.
It was in April of 1986 that the American fish processors first complained about Canada's actions which affect the fisheries, the fact that we were not allowing the export of our product and yet we were importing some of their product. At the time, it was calculated if it were reduced to dollars, the total claim for damage would be in the neighbourhood of $3 million.
In September of 1986, American trade negotiators complained to GATT. In November of 1987, a GATT panel upheld the American complaint and referred it to the full GATT council.
The minister took this seriously because in the same month, the same minister is quoted in Hansard as saying that many members of GATT use export controls to ensure adequate supply of raw materials for their own domestic industries. He believed and speculated that representatives of nations who sat on the GATT panel used such export controls, and what we have here is a panel recommendation which will, in all likelihood, be overturned by the GATT council of which we are a member. We will be opposing that recommendation when it reaches the GATT council.
I can find nothing that tells me that the minister and the government did actually oppose those recommendations at the GATT council. Perhaps I can be corrected on that. I would hope that the minister can assure me that Canada did actually protest it. As I say, to the best of my knowledge, I have seen nothing to that effect.
It would appear as though Canada decided to roll over and play dead with respect to the GATT decision. We could have objected. We could have vetoed it, but we decided to accept it because we had a solution.
Before the final ruling of the GATT council in March of 1988 supposed to do everything to protect Canada. If
it was going to protect Canada, it had to hurt the United States, and you know very well that the United States was not in it to get hurt. It was in it to get even. Getting even was its goal and getting even is what it has achieved.
In any case, on March 21, 1988, the same minister and the then Minister for International Trade announced that Canada will not veto the GATT ruling. The GATT council accepted the panel report on March 21, 1988. I have the minister's attention now, I think. Earlier he said March of 1987.
On April 25,1989, under U.S. pressure to abandon the processing requirements for B.C., the Minister for International Trade ignored the recommendations of the fishing industry working group representing all sectors of the B.C. industry and announced that the government will proceed with a landing requirement for B.C. salmon and herring. All the new regulations require that fish be brought to shore at a licensed landing station before they can be exported unprocessed.
I said earlier that the extent of the damage with respect to the first complaint was calculated to be some $3 million. We are talking about an industry with gross revenues, three years ago-and the minister himself has said that this is a record year in the past nine decades- of $747 million. That was in 1986. We do not have the figures for 1989, but they have to be over $1 billion. We are talking about a big industry; $573 million of $747 million is generated by export sales, a very important industry from the point of view of exports. If we are looking at a $3 million penalty, it would be very easy to swallow to maintain the long-term future of such an industry. It had an annual payroll, again three years ago, of $125 million; $79 million paid annually in taxes. It is important that we do maintain this industry. Employment is important, but the long range perpetuation of the resource is of even greater importance. It is the fourth largest industry in B.C.
When it comes to employment, I think it is significant that most of the employees in the processing industry are women, many of whom are native women or members of visible minorities.
The processing requirements, the industry argues, the union argue, and the opposition generally argues, were necessary to ensure proper conservation and management of the fish stocks. It is impossible to accomplish
October 19, 1989

that if the product, the roundfish, is sold to U.S. processors.
The minister talked about the free trade panel upholding our sovereignty. As I suggested yesterday, I did not know that our sovereignty was under question, but obviously it is. The answer is, yes, we are a sovereign nation, as long as we let the Americans tell us what proportion of our product should be exported in round.

I am told that there were three Canadians on the panel.
It is also important, since the member raised that question, that Canada could have asked for further hearings with the passing of one of the Canadian members of that panel and his replacement with another member, to hear additional evidence which was accumulated since that time. There was a strike and we had certain information. Canada chose not to ask for those additional hearings. We let it go through.
I have yet to see a copy of the preliminary report. All I have seen is the American summary of it in Inside U.S. Trade, which was published September 15, the day the report was first talked about up here, and the day I was criticized for making it public. The Minister was not reading, the government was not reading, they did not know it was in the public papers. However, we found out by reading public papers what the preliminary report was. We have yet to see a copy of it. I assume it is similar, if not the same, because no one has suggested there have been any changes. We could have tried to get changes, but we chose not to. Presumably, the minister or his ministry, or somebody, must have some kind of solution in mind. The solution is not to let the Americans tell us what proportion of the fish can be sold over the side of the boat to other boats, to other processors.
The landing requirements refer to all five species of salmon. I have seen one figure that we are talking about, possibly some 1,200 separate runs of salmon up the-

The minister says it is 4,500. I am glad to have the figure. I was looking for it and I could not even find the 1,200 figure this morning. There are 4,500 runs of salmon that do not all go up the rivers the same day. They go in different periods. If you are going to get

sufficient escapement of each of those 4,500 runs, you have to make sure that that is happening on a day-to-day basis. We know what fish are being landed in British Columbia promptly. I have seen a suggestion in one of the papers this morning from one of the processing industry people asking how we can keep track of individual sales from a fish boat to an American packer if we do not bother to keep records, if they forget to tell somebody that they caught these fish and do not bother to say where they got them from, how many they caught, and what species they were. How are we going to know early in the fishing season how much is going to be 20 per cent? If the minister had estimated at the beginning of the 1989 fishing season- and I think he has already said that that is the best sockeye run in some 84 or 87 years-what 20 per cent would be he would have been 100 per cent out because that much more sockeye showed up than he expected, so there would have been only 10 per cent, which is better for us.
But suppose the estimates were the other way around. Suppose they were only half as many came back as were expected. It would have meant a serious depletion of the early runs to the extent that they could have been so weakened that they would have been wiped out. That is serious. We have no idea when each one of the 4,500 runs is going to go up the rivers and which river each one is going up. We have no idea unless we are keeping track of those fish on a day-to-day basis.
It is important for conservation that we have that control. There is a solution. Both the industry and the union are proposing the same solution, namely, that we insist on landing 100 per cent of our salmon in B.C. Let us negotiate the penalty. There would be a penalty because it is going to cost the American processors-if they want to buy 10 per cent or 11 per cent of our fish, even up to 20 per cent-a couple of cents a pound to truck those fish from our landing stations down to their processing stations. It is very little per fish, very little for

speechtext: You are assuming it is the same.

The minister interjects by saying I am assuming it is the same. In light of his lack of any comments to the contrary up to this point and in light of the fact that the government did not ask for any further hearings even though there was a new member on the panel, I think it is a fairly safe assumption. If the minister cares to tell me that it is not the same, I will not accept that. If he says it is not similar, then I would be pleased to hear it. I would like to hear what the differences are. Maybe we can approach Inside U.S. Trade and ask for a copy of the preliminary report on which it based this summary so we will know exactly what was in it. We seem to have precious little luck in trying to get it out of any government circle here in Ottawa.
I will admit we got the final one. We could not find out when we were going to get it, how we were going to get it, or where we were going to get it but we were told it would be released on Monday. That was as much as we could get.
Although the press got copies of the press release from the trade minister's office and from the Minister of Fisheries' office, we had a great deal of difficulty even getting a copy of that press release. We finally got one by fax from a member of the press gallery. There are ways of getting these things if one works at it hard enough.
Employment is important. As I said, there are mainly women in the processing industry, mainly native workers and visible minorities, immigrant women or second generation immigrant women. The government talks about all the jobs that are being created by free trade. I am talking about some 15,000 part-time jobs in the height of the season that could be lost. This is the beginning.
If the Americans say they will let us limit the export to 10 per cent of roundfish this year, what is to stop them from coming back next year and saying it has to be 15, and year by year changing it? Nothing at all. There is nothing in the deal. We are not signing a contract that it is going to be 10, 11 or 12 per cent, or whatever figure, from now until the end of the free trade agreement. We are simply saying that for today that is the rule. There is nothing stopping them from changing that.
It could mean wiping out the fishing and the processing industries in B.C. and the subsequent loss of all those jobs. All the jobs that free trade creates, such as making and serving coffee in the tourism industry, is not going to help the people in the communities that are going to be totally shut down because fishing is the only source of employment in those communities. It is a serious matter.
The government has, up to this point, abandoned the fishing industry on the west coast. It made a deal for the east coast. That deal, as I think I said yesterday, is not worth the paper it is written on. That deal will not stand up long under attack if the Americans decide to go after it.
There is a solution, and I have pointed out the details of that solution. The minister acknowledged that he was aware of that solution. Ele knows that the industry supports it and he knows that the union supports it officially, because he was nodding as I was describing the possible way to resolve the situation, a way that would maintain employment. The minister has said in the past that it is important to maintain historic jobs, I think were his words. Another time he said he did not mean the same jobs. He said he would not allow jobs historically established to be threatened.
I do not know what other kinds of jobs there could be other than the jobs in the processing industry which have been historically established. The minister made it quite clear that what he had in mind was preserving the historically established jobs. He can do that with the solution I described.
Even with every possible control, even by catching every fish and knowing exactly what run each one comes from, we still cannot be perfect, but at least we will know how many fish come back in a season. We can ensure the optimum escapement on a day-to-day basis if we know what is happening on a day-to-day basis. The only way

we can know that is by insisting that 100 per cent of our resource is caught and landed in British Columbia so that we can count it, identify it and grade it. Then we will know.
I am concerned, as I have said, and as the Leader of the New Democratic Party has said, that it is not just fish. If the Americans say that they have access to our fish resource, that we cannot deny them the right to come into this country and buy them, how can we possibly maintain our position with respect to round logs? How can Ontario possibly retain its position with respect to mineral ores which the province of Ontario now says have to be processed to some extent before they are shipped out? This is one renewable resource, and certainly B.C. timber and timber from other provinces is another. Are they not in as much jeopardy as are the fish resources, particularly on the west coast and eventually the east coast, if we accept this meekly?
I urge the minister to accept the solution proposed by the fisheries industry council and by the fishermen's union.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, while I enjoyed listening to the member from Nanaimo, I do have a few comments I would like to make, and perhaps I will ask a question or two. First of all, he pointed out that it was mainly minorities and women who worked in fish canneries, as though there was something wrong with working in a fish cannery in the first place and they had been relegated to second class status.
Shame!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Here is the noble NDP shouting us down again. I remember that when I worked in fish canneries, the people working there were mainly from minorities. I was one of those who was from a minority group working in the fish cannery.
I noticed that the hon. member said the government should treat this decision on the FTA with caution. At the same time, the minister is criticized for saying that there are 30 days in which to make a decision. Now, the member cannot have it both ways. He cannot say decide today, but be cautious. We can count on it, for sure, that if the minister made a decision today, he would be criticized for not being cautious, for being hasty. Somehow, the member wants it both ways.
Supply
Well, now the NDP are taking coaching lessons from the hon. member from Newfoundland. It needs all the help it can get, even from the member from Newfoundland.
Even from where?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: From this member here, the member from Newfoundland. What is his riding?
Which one?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
He represents all of Newfoundland.
The other thing that I want to talk about is the member's oversimplification of the change that has taken place in the industry. He pointed out that he grew up in British Columbia as I did. He has lived there a little longer than I have. I hope to catch up to him some day if normal events take their course.
He pointed out that in the early days of fishing, there was unlimited access to the resource. You could pretty well go fishing at will. I remember those days when the fishing industry was shut down mainly on weekends. The rest of the time it was open. I remember the days when you could pretty well on a Monday walk across the Fraser River on the gillnetters that were fishing the river at that time.
I guess he is suggesting that because you could fish constantly 50 years ago and you cannot fish constantly today that somehow there has been a depletion of the resource and that is a sign of mismanagement. If he will do only one thing and that is check the tonnage figures of the total catch of the 1930s and 1940s and compare them with the figures for the 1970s and 1980s, I think the member from Nanaimo will agree that there has been a steady progression in the increase of tonnage. Just because there is not constant and daily fishing and it is not open season in the fishing industry does not mean that the resource has been depleted. Maybe it is a sign of careful management rather than depletion.
For example, does he not agree that there has been a change in technology? In the days that he harkens to of the 1930s and 1940s in the fishing industry, fishing was restricted mostly to gillnetters of about 30 feet long. There was no sonar, there was no radar, there was no radio to speak of, none of the high technology. There were no seiners out there, no trailers out there of any size or consequence.

Supply
Today, the fish do not stand a chance when you have the kind of technology that can track them all over the place. There has been a change in technology on the fishing side of it. There has also been a change in technology on the processing and marketing side of it. In the days when he and I worked in the industry, it was all canning.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: Question!

In those days, it had to be canned immediately. Today, if the processing plants cannot keep up with the catch coming into port, they can freeze it and can it a little later on, as we saw on television the other night when the worker was interviewed regarding her opinion on the FTA decision.
There is also a different market where the fish are quick frozen today and then flown to Europe. The whole industry has changed.
I would like to ask the member if he does not accept the notion that maybe he oversimplified the problem by saying that just because things today are not the way they used to be, there has been a depletion of the resource and a mismanagement of the resource. Would he not accept the fact that the increase in total tonnage that we have seen is a result of the successful management begun in the government previous to ours in the Salmo-nid Enhancement Program and enhanced by this Minister of Fisheries when he doubled investment in the Salmonid Enhancement Program several years ago? He doubled the commitment to make sure of the future of the resource. Would he not kindly agree that he oversimplified the case when he spoke earlier?

Madam Speaker, I was afraid that the member would not leave me any time at all for a response.
First, with respect to women working in the canneries, either I was not speaking clearly or the member was not listening, but my point was that in the small communities that I said were going to closed down totally without these small canneries and I know that they are closing anyway, there are mainly women working in them because that is the only opportunity for employment for
people in those communities. It is not a case of demeaning the role that they are playing.
With respect to my advising caution, I do not recall using that word. I did suggest to the minister what the Canadian reaction should be, but I would say to the member that it is not three days that have gone by, the minister has had the report in his hand for 36 days, and there are only 26 days left.
With respect to depletion of resources, the point that I was trying to make, and again I think the member may have been distracted, is that there has been an increase with some species. There has been a serious diminish-ment in the quantity of the resource for many other species. Can you say that we are good managers of some species because they happen to be the ones that have increased, and say that we are good managers of the others that are being wiped out? Would the member say that maybe there was some good fortune? Also, the member knows that there was a serious incident on the Fraser River that has taken quite some time, the most important run of all.
Yes, there has been good management. I accepted that. I mentioned that, but I said that in some instances, unfortunately we rely on the opinion of experts who do not always know and who do not, at least in my experience, listen to the fishermen who are out there.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my colleagues on the other side of the House, my colleague on this side of the House and the member who just spoke have been focusing on the situation on the west coast.
One of the reasons we in this party put down the motion in the name of the hon. member for Beausejour, the fisheries critic for the official opposition, was that we have been alarmed by an attitude of the minister of fisheries who insists on telling us that the fishery is in great shape, the catch has been bountiful, profits have been high.
I want to tell the minister of fisheries, who is in the House, that in my riding of Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte, on the Baie Verte Peninsula, and in the Bay of Islands area, the entire west coast of the province, there are 1,200 fishermen this year who have found the fishery so poor that they have not even earned enough insurable weeks of earnings to qualify for unemployment insurance. When we have asked, for a response program for those primary producers, the same as the government has, rightly and with our applause, responded to the

plight of primary producers called farmers, so far, all we have heard is that the fishery is in good shape.
Not in anger but in desperation, I take this opportunity to say to the minister that these people are in desperate shape. He knows they cannot qualify for unemployment insurance, until November 15. He knows that the social welfare program does not kick in until the end of that qualifying period, and he knows that right now there is a shortage of bread and butter on the table. That is not an exaggeration.
I use this opportunity to ask the minister of fisheries to get together with the Minister of Employment and Immigration to give us this year a response to a desperate human plight, a response that cannot wait until a week or two before Christmas, one that needs to be dealt with now. I make that plea in the name of all of those fishermen, and fish plant workers, primarily women, who today have no income and no prospect of income as we enter the Christmas season, until some time perhaps nearing the new year. Let us not leave them hanging high and dry, hungry and cold again this year, please.

Mr. Speaker, for my riding of Samia-Lambton and others bordering the Great Lakes, the recent commitment of $125 million in new federal government funds to help clean up and preserve the Great Lakes is a much welcomed announcement.
October 19, 1989

The doubling of federal funds, I believe, constitutes an important step forward in our long-term effort to protect this vital ecosystem.
Today, the Great Lakes provide drinking water, recreation, and to a very significant extent, the economic underpinnings for some 35 million Canadians and Americans.
In the wake of this new action plan, there still remains much to do on many levels. Environmental issues and concerns are not simple problems which can be addressed unilaterally or through a single program or initiative.
While I do recognize that a lot of work has already been done at the provincial and municipal level, much more must be done. Certainly, both have an integral role to play in the upgrading of the current sewage treatment and drainage systems.
At the same time, I call on individual Canadians to actively participate in the clean-up initiative. They too have a vital role to play. Every one of us can and must make a better accounting of what type of waste and by-products we are discharging into the environment. For this to work, Canadians must be part of the solution, not the problem.
In the end, by all of us working together in a constructive and concerted fashion, I strongly believe that we can protect and upgrade our Great Lakes.

Mr. Speaker, this week we observe National Co-operative Week. The purpose of this annual event is to remind Canadians of the role co-operatives have played and continue to play on our society and our economy.
All together Canadian co-ops have some $70 billion in assets and conduct about $14 billion in annual business. Twelve million Canadians are members of one or more co-ops. Co-ops are good citizens. They are involved in such things as famine relief overseas and helping the needy at home.
Co-ops are major players in the grain trade, the dairy industry and the poultry sector. They are also involved in almost every other part of the economy from Inuit handicrafts to computer software.
Our government created the co-operative secretariat in 1987 to act as a focal point for the government's role in the sector. Then we set up the advisory committee that gives co-ops an opportunity to advise the government on the potential impact of government policies on co-operatives.
We have also set up an interdepartmental committee to ensure that all government departments are aware of the concerns of the co-op sector and to take them into account in drafting new policies.
I am sure I speak for all members of Parliament when I offer my best wishes to the Canadian co-op sector.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we celebrate international savings and credit co-operative day. Canada's credit unions go back to 1900, when Alphonse Desjardins founded the Caisse populaire de Levis with 130 members. Since then, the Federation des caisses populaires Desjardins has become Canada's sixth most important financial institution. It has over 4 million members and nearly $40 billion in assets.
Today, there are credit unions in every province and in almost all communities in this country. Each one is an independent agency that belongs to its members and is managed by them. In addition to their economic role, credit unions, like other co-operatives, play a vital social role in the communities they serve. That this House condemn the government's mismanagement, lack

The
fishery is of vital importance in almost every single community, 158 of them, which make up the great riding of Burin-St. George's, along the south coast of Newfoundland, along the southwest corner and up a bit of the west coast.
It is for that reason, among others, that I am delighted to rise and support the motion put forward by my colleague from New Brunswick, from the riding of Beausejour, which calls on this House to condemn the government's mismanagement, lack of leadership, incompetence and negligence that have placed Canada's fishing communities and workers in unparalled jeopardy.
First of all, I could not have said it better myself. I believe when members of this House reflect on what the gentleman from New Brunswick has asked the House to concur in, they will rush to his support because this government, as the motion implies, has been lacking in leadership, has been incompetent, has been negligent and has placed Canada's fishing communities, including many of dozens of such communities in my own riding, in unparalled jeopardy.
I can say to the Minister of Fisheries I can support that resolution with great relish.
I listened to the Minister of Fisheries earlier in the debate. In response to my good friend from Gander-Grand Falls, in talking about the issue of overfishing, he used this tell-tale phrase: "We fixed that". Yes, he certainly fixed that, and I will show you how he fixed it.
I have here a document from the Government of Newfoundland, published last week and given to the Government of Canada some weeks ago, entitled "Resource Crisis in the Newfoundland Fishery". On Page 5 of that document, the Government of Newfoundland shows just how the Minister of Fisheries here in this House fixed the question of overfishing. I will give you a couple of quick figures.
The NAFO allocation for the European Community in 1986 was 26,295 metric tonnes. Those same countries in the EEC took in that year 160,000 metric tonnes or about six times what the catch was supposed to be. The next year the quota was 25,205 metric tonnes. The EEC countries, particularly Spain and Portugal, took 134,000 metric tonnes.
I say to the Minister of Fisheries that he fixed it all right. He, together with the Prime Minister, the member for St. John's West and the Minister of Trade, allowed Spain and Portugal to walk all over us during those years and he brags today that he fixed the over-fishing issue. He tends to be very selective when he is quoting statistics, when he is quoting from newspapers, just as he was this morning on the west coast issue. I wish I had time to talk about that because although it is the west coast of Canada, the trade ruling of a few days ago has a lot of implications for the fishery on the east coast of Canada, including the one in Newfoundland.
Just in passing, to make the point, the minister this morning told us that the ruling was being welcomed with open arms by everybody out there. He is being very selective. Why did he not read all the headlines? Why did he not read the one in the Ottawa Citizen of October 19, which said: "Fish Industry Slams Trade Ruling". Why did he not go to the newspaper in Quebec city, Le Soled, which declares "Le saumon fait hurles". A rough translation, I believe, is "This ruling is an outrage". That is about the ruling the minister told us this morning was the best thing since sliced bread. It is only a matter of time before that kind of ruling, where the Americans can do what they want with our fish, begins getting applied to the east coast fishery, including the fishery in Burin-St. George's.
I listened with great interest this morning to the Minister of Fisheries. One of the things he said about me during his debate was that I am exaggerating the problem
October 19, 1989

that I am spreading fear among the fishermen. He thinks everybody out there is wrong except him.
Let us look again at the report prepared by the Government of Newfoundland after a lot of research, where the Government of Newfoundland tells us and I quote: "The potential direct employment losses anticipated in the fishery in Newfoundland in 1990 are as follows: Offshore sector, 1,400 jobs; inshore sector, 800''.
